questions.question: Pasteurization process is not a sterilization process. Explain the statement
questions.solution_html:
• Sterilization is a drastic process that involves heating food or objects to
  • temperatures above 100°C (212°F), often using an autoclave (steam under pressure).
  • This intense heat is designed to destroy all microorganisms and their
  • resilient bacterial spores. Products are rendered completely sterile and can be stored
  • at room temperature for a long duration, often many months, until the package is
  • opened.
  • Pasteurization uses milder heat treatments, typically below 100°C , for a specific
  • duration (e.g., heating milk to 72°C for 15 seconds). The objective is to target and
  • destroy pathogenic bacteria and inactivate spoilage enzymes, making the food safe for
  • consumption and extending its shelf life by a few weeks. However, the less resistant
  • forms and some heat-resistant spores can survive the process.
  • (Answer 1 questions)
questions.source_exam: First Semester MGU-UGP/MGU-BBA/MGU-BCA Honours Examinations November 2025

questions.question: How does irradiation affect the nutritive value of milk ?
questions.solution_html:
• Irradiation significantly improves milk safety by killing microbes but causes minor
  • nutritional changes, primarily affecting some vitamins (like B vitamins) and amino
  • acids (like tryptophan, glutamic acid) , similar to heat pasteurization, with effects
  • depending heavily on the dose; however, overall protein digestibility and biological
  • value remain largely unaffected or slightly reduced, and with proper gassing
  • (nitrogen), lipid peroxidation is minimized, ensuring it remains safe and nutritious
  • comparable to heat-treated milk

questions.question: Write a note on toned milk processing ?
questions.solution_html:
• Toned milk is made by combining whole milk (like buffalo or cow's milk) with skim milk or
  • skim milk powder and water . This mixture is then standardized to a specific fat content
  • typically around 3%, while maintaining essential nutrients like calcium and protein. The
  • process reduces the fat content of the milk, making it lower in calories and a popular
  • alternative to full-fat milk.

questions.question: Write down the steps involved in the pasteurization of milk ?
questions.solution_html:
• Pasteurization of milk is heating it to a specific temperature for a set time to kill harmful
  • bacteria like Salmonella, E. coli, and Listeria, making it safe to drink and extending its shelf
  • life, without significantly reducing nutrients . Common methods include HTST (High
  • Temperature Short -Time), heating to ~72°C (161°F) for 15 seconds, and UHT ( Ultra
  • High Temperature ), using much higher temps for shorter times for longer shelf stability.
  • This process is crucial for public health, preventing diseases like tuberculosis and typhoid
  • and ensures milk remains a safe, nutrient-rich food.

questions.question: Write a note on homogenizer and factors influenzing homogenization ?
questions.solution_html:
• A homogenizer is a mechanical device that creates a stable and uniform mixture (an
  • emulsion or suspension) by forcing a liquid through a narrow opening under high pressure .
  • This process, known as homogenization, breaks down large particles or droplets (like the fat
  • globules in milk) into much smaller, uniformly dispersed sizes, primarily through the
  • physical principles of turbulence, cavitation, and shearing.
  • Factors Affecting Homogenization Efficiency
  • The effectiveness of the homogenization process can be influenced by several key factors
  • Pressure: This is a critical factor; higher pressure generally results in smaller particles and a
  • more stable emulsion. Pressures for milk typically range from 100 to 250 bar (1500 -3600
  • psi).
  • Temperature: The product must be heated above the melting point of its fat (typically 55
  • 80°C for milk) to ensure the fat is in a liquid state for proper subdivision. Homogenizing raw
  • milk without prior heating can lead to rapid flavour deterioration due to enzyme (lipase)
  • activity.
  • Product Composition (Fat/Protein Content) : Products with high fat content (e.g., cream)
  • are more difficult to homogenize efficiently because there may be insufficient protein
  • available in the milk serum to form a new protective membrane around the increased surface
  • area of small fat globules, leading to clumping.
  • Homogenizer Design/Configuration
  • o Valve type (e.g., radial, axial flow) affects efficiency and flow characteristics.
  • o Single-stage vs. Two -stage: Two-stage homogenization uses a second, lower -pressure stage
  • to break up any fat globule clusters that form immediately after the first stage, improving
  • overall stability.
  • Flow Rate/Processing Time: Higher flow rates can result in lower efficiency if the particles
  • do not spend enough time within the high-shear zone.
  • Viscosity: The viscosity of the liquid affects how easily droplets can be deformed and broken
  • apart by turbulent forces.
